title: T145 PNC - No Man Dies With Half His Desire (II) — Controversy as Partial Vision (1 seg)
hebrewTitle: אֵין אָדָם מֵת בַּחֲצִי יָמָיו (ב) — מַחֲלֹקֶת כְּרְאִיָּה חֶלְקִית
author: Petten Nanach

beginner.en: Again: 'No man dies with half his desire in his hand' (Midrash Rabbah, Kohelet 1). This second teaching on the same phrase focuses on a different aspect: controversy (machloket). The Targum on 'and they became owners of arrows against him' (Genesis 49:23, regarding Joseph's brothers) translates as: 'they became owners of division (machloket).' The person who holds onto his desire — who refuses to let the divine will have its full expression and insists on his own partial vision — becomes an 'owner of division.' Controversy and dispute arise when people cling to their partial perspective as if it were the whole. The teaching: releasing one's half-grasped desire, surrendering the partial view, is the opposite of machloket. True spiritual unity comes from letting go of the insistence on one's own incomplete picture.

intermediate.en: Same phrase, different aspect: machloket (controversy). Targum Gen 49:23: Joseph's brothers = 'owners of division.' Person who clings to his partial desire = 'owner of division.' Controversy = clinging to partial perspective as if whole. Release of half-grasped desire = opposite of machloket. Spiritual unity = letting go of incomplete picture.
intermediate.he: אוֹתוֹ בִּטּוּי, עִנְיָן נוֹסָף: מַחֲלֹקֶת. תַּרְגּוּם בר' מ"ט:כג: 'בַּעֲלֵי פְלֻגְּתָא.' הַנִּאָחֵז בְּחֶשְׁקוֹ הַחֶלְקִי = 'בַּעַל מַחֲלֹקֶת.' מַחֲלֹקֶת = הֶחָזָקָה בִּפֶּרְסְפֶּקְטִיבָה חֶלְקִית כְּאִילּוּ הִיא הַכֹּל. שִׁחְרוּר מֵחֶשֶׁק חֶלְקִי = הֵפֶךְ מַחֲלֹקֶת. אַחְדוּת רוּחָנִית = עֲזִיבַת הַתּמוּנָה הֶחֶלְקִית.
